newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian lek calm, seen steady to election.
newsitem.headline: Albanian lek calm, seen steady to election.

text.p: Albania's lek currency eased slightly against the dollar on Tuesday but dealers said the embattled lek was likely to remain steady in the run-up to the Balkan nation's early parliamentary elections on June 29.

The lek fell to 182 to the dollar on Tuesday from 181 on Monday, dealers said. It was still valued at 104 to the dollar in January, retaining some strength before the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes.
Dealers saw scope for the lek to fluctuate slightly, but said it would remain around the same level until the poll with activity stagnant and no market-moving factors in sight.
"It has been fixed around this level and is now making small moves on the basis of supply and demand," a street dealer in Tirana's market said.
He added that the lek had also eased slightly against the German mark, Italian lira and the Greek drachma.
A commercial banker said the volume of trade had fallen, the market was stagnating and a further devaluation of the lek was not likely despite Albania's continued chaos.
"Since the central bank intervened the rate has been fixed at around 180 leks to the dollar," the banker said.
The central bank intervened at the end of May to stop the lek from plunging past a record low of 194 leks to the dollar, and it then gradually firmed to 176.
The lek lost a little ground last week after reports a fresh quantity of money would come onto the market, with some 54 tonnes of currency notes imported into Albania.
But the central bank said the imported notes had been ordered about a year and a half ago, long before Albania's investment schemes crisis, and offered more security features.
An official said the bank would inform the public before it put the new notes into circulation, and the bank has denied any suggestion the new money could be circulated without control.
Another street dealer said business was slack, curbed as usual by torrid summer heat, and merchants had been less active than usual amid Albania's security concerns.
"The lek will go up and down by two or three leks but it will remain about this level," the dealer, Fatmir, said.
